How SKY-001 Beats Prompt-Based Methods Step-By-Step

STAGE 1

Parallel Explorations Through World Modeling

Our model converts a 2D image or text prompt into several rough 3D assets at once. This lets you instantly explore different visual directions and pick the best foundation before diving into details.

STAGE 2

Recursive Diffusion-Based 3D Decomposition

Once selected, it breaks down the high-level designs into smaller, individual parts, from large structural pieces all the way down to tiny screws and fasteners. By working layer by layer, our model keeps complex designs organized and easy to build, excelling in long horizon planning.

STAGE 3

Multi-step 2D to 3D Latent World Model

It brings each part to life by recreating how a real designer works step-by-step. It starts by drawing precise 2D sketches stroke-by-stroke, then stretches, cuts, or shapes those sketches into finished 3D objects.

STAGE 4

3D Construction World Model

Finally, it assembles all the parts, layer by layer again, in hierarchical order into a complete 3D assembly that you can visualize immediately in standard 3D asset viewer

Introducing SKY-001:
The First World Model
for Engineering

The last decade of AI has been defined by language models that can reason, write code and solve increasingly complex problems. Engineering in the physical world is still hard for them. A design that reads well in text may not be geometrically accurate, physically feasible or manufacturable: engineering means keeping spatial relationships and constraints consistent across thousands of interconnected components, and language is an inefficient medium for that kind of reasoning.

How will Enterprise World Models lead to Eudaimonia and Global Prosperity?

In their 2014 book The Second Machine Age, academics Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee identify the productivity explosion of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as the First Machine Age. Whereas technological innovations before the Industrial MRevolution were primarily augmentations of an individual’s capacity, the Industrial Revolution created tools that far exceeded their maker. From the synergy of the productive ensemble came such material abundance that a person living after was to a person living before almost as if an entirely new species.

Why Large Language Models Are Not Continual Learners

Enterprise AI is moving from static tools to autonomous agents, where systems are asked to make sequential decisions across supply chains, warehouse operations, and production planning, not just once, but continuously, across environments that shift over time. This raises a question that benchmark leaderboards do not answer: can an AI agent that performs well today continue to perform well as conditions change? Can it detect when its operating environment has drifted, adapt its behaviour in response, and do so reliably across many such shifts? These are the defining challenges of continual learning, and they are poorly represented in existing evaluation frameworks.

Introducing OpenRCT2: Why can Claude & GPT ace ARC-AGI but fail running a business?

Human life has long been dominated by work and commerce – the means by which we meet our physical needs. Even children’s toys reflect this, be it a toy stethoscope or a video game like Roller Coaster Tycoon. Given this focus, it is unsurprising that our earliest conceptions of artificially intelligent creatures also revolve around these themes. From the hardworking golem of Jewish folklore to the introduction of the word “robot” in the play R.U.R. (derived from the Czech word for “serf”), these intelligent machines were portrayed as economic engines, albeit unreliable ones. Consequently, it is only natural that there is a deep interest in applying modern machine learning methods to previously impossible tasks, namely business management itself. However, this has proven to be extremely challenging. Over the past year, Anthropic has tested Claude’s ability to operate a vending machine; this culminated in December of last year when they deployed their system to the Wall Street Journal’s newsroom. It was bankrupt within a week. Among other issues, it bought a live pet fish, repeatedly set prices to zero, and briefly believed it was a Soviet vending machine in the basement of Moscow U.

WOW: Bridging the AI Safety gap in Enterprises via World Models

AI systems now have higher penetration in the enterprise than a year ago and are now moving from experimental tools to decision-making agents. As a result, the question of AI safety is rapidly shifting from a research concern to a practical necessity. In enterprise settings, AI systems don’t just generate text or recommendations; they initiate actions that modify databases, trigger workflows and affect real users. Failures in these environments can be catastrophic for the enterprise. A single incorrect action can cascade across interconnected systems, violating business constraints or creating compliance and security risks. AI safety in the enterprise is fundamentally about ensuring reliable behavior under complexity, partial information, and long-horizon consequences.

Pioneering steps towards building World Models for Planning in Enterprise

Human planning first emerged as a basic survival mechanism in prehistoric times, millions of years ago. In order to thrive, hunter gatherer societies needed to coordinate group hunts and migrations in search of food and resources. These early forms of planning were rudimentary and focussed on the short-term, limited by the ability of individual humans to remember past events, recognize patterns and imagine possible future events.

MAPS: Building the foundations of an 'AI CEO'

Over the course of the last year, our team at Skyfall has started to  build the foundations of an ‘AI CEO’. For enterprise, an AI CEO addresses the fundamental bottleneck lacking in modern enterprises - cognitive scale. Corporations operate across dozens of geographies, with thousands of employees and even more processes and workflows. Yet, they rely on a small leadership team to synthesize all of this information with the CEO being the main decision maker. An AI CEO could simulate potential scenarios, anticipate financial and geo-political disruptions, and continuously optimize decisions across the entire enterprise. We believe that an AI CEO has tremendous potential for transforming how enterprises have operated thus far, bringing enormous efficiencies in scale with respect to cognitive decision making within enterprises.
